newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo NBY may cut discount rate in June-c.banker.
newsitem.headline: Yugo NBY may cut discount rate in June-c.banker.

text.p: The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) may cut again its discount rate in June to reduce the gap between its base rate and the level of inflation, the NBY Vice-Governor Ratko Banovic said on Friday.

"I expect the discount rate to go down in June. Already in April we had a zero inflation. If that is repeated in May there is no reason to keep such big real margin (between the discount rate and inflation)," Banovic told Reuters in an interview.

This would be the second reduction in the central bank's key rate this year. The NBY first sliced the discount rate in March to 2.5 percent per month after keeping it steady at a monthly 4.5 percent since June 1996.

"In our 1997 monetary policy, the discount rate has been chosen as an instrument for monetary regulation and as the central bank's base rate in regulating the amount of cash in circulation," Banovic said.

The discount rate must remain positive in real terms regardless of market developments and must be a key reference rate for commercial bank lending rates. The level of the rate depends on retail price increases and interest rates on the local financial market, he added.

The sharp cut in the discount rate in March forced some big commercial banks to follow suit and cut down their base lending rates to between 3.00 and 3.25 percent per month from a previous monthly 5.85 percent.
In its 1997 monetary policy paper, the NBY said only banks which closely followed the central bank's interest rate policy could expect some help at times of liquidity crisis.

Apart from qualifying for the NBY's help, banks were forced to cut their lending rates also because of another regulation according to which interest rates, exceeding the discount rate by more than 30 percent, are subject to a 10 percent tax.
However, witty commercial bankers are now compensating lower rates with charging for "special services fees".
Banovic said for the time being commercial lending rates could not go down any further until overall economic situation improves.
"High bank lending rates result from entire economic situation. Banks need to have some way to cover losses and high costs," the vice-governor said.
"But if we find an adequate way to finance banks' dubious assets, those interest rates would become a more realistic reflection of the price of money the banks are offering.
"At the same time, banks would be able to adjust their deposit rates and attract more money which would help them increase credit potential and ability to improve their liquidity," Banovic said.
Along with the discount rate, the monetary authorities will also review the reserve requirement regulation in June.

Currently, banks set aside 15 percent of their deposits and 15 percent of their interbank lending to meet the reserve requirement. But the money deposited with the NBY is split into two separate accounts on a 50-50 percent basis.

Half of the reserve requirement can be used at times of liquidity crisis, while another half establishes a fund for the Serbian Commodity Reserve Agency to finance grain stockpiling via its short-term bonds.

The split in the reserve requirement funds is effective until the end of June, when the Commodity Reserve Agency is obliged to redeem those bonds and the money will be back on the reserve requirement account, Banovic said.

"We have launched the reserve requirement last September as an instrument to regulate liquidity of the banking system. If we hadn't done that, banks would have faced liquidity collapse at the end of 1996," Banovic said.
If there was no reserve requirement as a way to establish banks' reserves, the central bank would be forced to print more money.

"We shall decide on the reserve requirement in June based on industry output, price movements, the dinar exchange rate, the level of M1 money supply, credit multiplication. We cannot remain tied down by some decisions for long. We make decisions every day or every ten days," Banovic said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
